query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy transition-metal catalysts used for oxygen redox reactions, the synergistic interaction among dissimilar active sites produces a distribution of intermediate adsorption energies that optimizes the binding of reactants (such as O2-derived species) without over-stabilizing them, thereby enhancing catalytic activity and selectivity compared to more uniform, conventional catalysts.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalyst comprising multiple transition metals that create heterogeneous active sites, alongside a conventional phase-separated binary alloy with similar overall metal content.
generation.intervention: Synthesize and compare two catalysts: (a) a high-entropy disordered alloy with a broad distribution of local electronic structures, and (b) a phase-separated alloy with more uniform active sites.
generation.conditions: Evaluation under operando conditions in Li–O2 battery setups where oxygen reduction (ORR) and oxygen evolution (OER) reactions govern performance; all tests conducted under identical temperature, pressure, and electrolyte conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Heterogeneous local electronic structures at the catalyst surface provided by dissimilar transition-metal centers.
generation.mechanism: The varied d-band centers and orbital occupancies in the high-entropy catalyst induce a range of adsorption energies for intermediate species (e.g., LiO2, Li2O2), where some sites stabilize the necessary intermediates while others prevent over-binding. This balance facilitates improved reaction kinetics and enhanced selectivity across multistep redox processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical operational conditions, the high-entropy catalyst will exhibit improved round-trip efficiency, enhanced reversibility in Li2O2 deposition/decomposition, and higher selectivity in oxygen redox reactions compared to the phase-separated binary alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (e.g., catalytic current density, cycle efficiency, and intermediate adsorption stability) observed for conventional binary/phase-separated catalysts under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold during oxygen redox reactions in Li–O2 battery environments where intermediate adsorption/desorption processes are critical; its applicability to other reaction types or at extreme conditions (e.g., very high/low temperatures) may vary.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in quantifying the precise contribution of individual heterogeneous sites due to potential confounding effects such as variations in surface area and catalyst morphology; additionally, decoupling the effects of electronic heterogeneity from mere increases in accessible active sites remains challenging.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one high-entropy alloy with a disordered mix of transition metals and one phase-separated binary alloy with similar overall metal content. Integrate each catalyst into identically fabricated Li–O2 battery cells. Monitor differences in ORR/OER kinetics, round-trip efficiency, and Li2O2 formation/decomposition.
measurements: In situ spectroscopic measurements to determine adsorption energy distributions of reaction intermediates.
Cyclic voltammetry and polarization studies to assess ORR/OER kinetics.
Battery performance metrics (e.g., round-trip efficiency, cycle stability).
Structural characterizations (XPS, TEM, EELS) to confirm the distribution of active sites.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy catalyst does not show statistically significant improvements in catalytic activity, selectivity, or efficiency in oxygen redox reactions compared to the phase-separated binary alloy under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Those intractable issues mainly lie in the sluggish oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER), closely related to the complex O2/Li2O2 redox chemistry in the air cathodes []. The reversibility of Li2O2 deposition/decomposition directly determines the performance of LOB, highlighting the necessity of ameliorating reaction kinetics through constructing well-tailored catalysts. It is widely accepted that catalyst activity depends substantially on the adsorption/desorption of intermediates on surface-active sites, which can be modulated via tuning orbital occupancy of active centers []. Various elaborate catalysts with d-block transition metals, as LiO2-affinity regulators, have been rapidly explored in recent years to boosting catalytic conversion of O2/Li2O2 in LOBs []. Despite the considerable optimization in catalytic kinetics, the functionality and availability of such catalysts still fall short of expectations, mainly due to the limited number of accessible active sites.

atalytic properties of monometals and conventional binary alloys can be understood and even predicted in terms of the electronic structures of the principal elements both experimentally and theoretically (i.e. d-band theory). However, due to the heterogeneity of the surface atoms in HEAs, the catalytic properties of HEAs might be not limited by one principle element anymore and the d-band center theory might not be able to describe the activity of HEAs. The neighbouring active sites with different local electronic structures in HEAs also provide the possibility for tuning the selectively in complex reactions. For example, Yao et al. reported that PdPtRhRuCe HEA nanoparticles (NPs) showed almost 100% selectivity towards ammonia synthesis while the phase-separated alloy only had less than 20% selectivity. We have found that IrOsPtPdRhRu could catalyse ethanol oxidation with a 12-electron process, although the single metals generally prompt a four-electron process at most. Löffler et al. found that Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni complex solid solution showed at least comparable catalytic activity to Pt in oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), in despite that none of its constituents had good ORR activity.
